Exam Blueprint (What Gets Tested)

The CDMP Data Governance & Stewardship Specialist exam is 100 questions, 90 minutes, 60% pass mark (70%+ also earns a "Mastery" designation). Like all CDMP Specialist exams, it draws roughly 70% from the specialty area (Data Governance, DMBOK2 Ch 3) and ~30% from supporting knowledge areas that connect to governance (Architecture, Data Quality, MDM, Metadata).

⚠️ Accuracy note: The per-topic percentages below are estimated emphasis derived from the structure and length of DMBOK2 Chapter 3 — they are NOT official DAMA-published topic weights. DAMA publishes the specialty/supporting split (~70/30) and the question count, but does not publish a granular per-subtopic breakdown. Treat these as a study-prioritization guide, not exact exam quotas. Action item: confirm the current official format on the DAMA/CDMP exam page before your exam, as DAMA periodically updates exam specifications.

Estimated study emphasis (for prioritization only):

Topic Area Est. Emphasis Source DMBOK2 Chapter
Data Governance Principles & Concepts ~20% Specialty Ch 3
DG Organization & Operating Models ~15% Specialty Ch 3
Data Stewardship ~15% Specialty Ch 3
Policies, Standards & Business Glossary ~10% Specialty Ch 3
DG Strategy, Metrics, Change Mgmt & Activities ~10% Specialty Ch 3
Specialty subtotal ~70% Specialty Ch 3
Related KAs (Architecture, DQ, MDM, Metadata) ~30% Supporting Ch 4, 11, 12, 13

Key insight: ~70% is Data Governance (Ch 3) at application depth; ~30% tests how the supporting KAs connect to and are governed by DG. This is why Week 6 covers deep DG governance of each related KA — not standalone KA theory. The ~30% supporting weight is more significant than a casual reading of "it's a DG exam" suggests, so don't under-invest in the Week 6 governance-integration sections.

17 Data Governance Activities — Detailed Reference

The 17 DG Activities are organized into 4 groups reflecting the lifecycle of DG program maturity: from initial planning and strategy to implementation and embedding into the organization. These are the operational units of governance work.

Group 1: Define Data Governance for the Organization (Planning)

Initial planning and readiness activities before building DG strategy.

# Activity Purpose
2.1 Define DG for the Organization Establish shared understanding of what DG means in your organization's context; align leadership and stakeholders on DG scope and objectives.
2.2 Perform Readiness Assessment Evaluate organization's current maturity in (1) data management, (2) capacity to change, (3) collaborative readiness, and (4) business alignment. Results inform strategy scope.
2.3 Perform Discovery and Business Alignment Understand current state — data flows, business processes, pain points, regulatory drivers. Identify where DG initiatives create most value.
2.4 Develop Organizational Touchpoints Map where DG interacts with IT, business units, finance, compliance, SDLC, procurement. Identify stakeholder groups and communication channels.

Group 2: Define the DG Strategy (Planning)

Strategy and framework design to guide DG implementation.

# Activity Purpose
2.5 Develop Data Governance Strategy Create DG vision, mission, goals, and business case. Align with enterprise strategy. Define target operating model (Centralized/Federated/Replicated).
2.6 Define the DG Operating Framework Document DG organizational structure, accountabilities, decision rights, escalation paths. Define the 5 DG bodies and their composition/authority.
2.7 Develop Goals, Principles, and Policies Establish DG principles that guide all activities. Draft foundational policies (data ownership, stewardship, quality, security, privacy).
2.8 Underwrite Data Management Projects DG reviews and approves data management projects (MDM, DQ, architecture, integration) to ensure they align with DG strategy and standards.
2.9 Engage Change Management Plan OCM for DG rollout using ADKAR framework. Manage resistance, build awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement. Track adoption.
2.10 Engage in Issue Management Establish issue management process for conflicts (authority, compliance, quality, contracts, etc.). Define escalation paths (Stewardship Teams → DGC → Steering Committee).
2.11 Assess Regulatory Compliance Requirements Identify regulations that apply (BCBS 239, CPG 235, PCI-DSS, Solvency II, privacy laws, etc.). Map compliance obligations to DG policies and responsibilities.

Group 3: Implement Data Governance (Operations)

Day-to-day operational execution of governance.

# Activity Purpose
2.12 Implement Data Governance Execute DG policies, standards, and procedures. Operationalize stewardship teams, issue escalation, and compliance monitoring. Roll out training and tools.
2.13 Sponsor Data Standards and Procedures DG promotes adoption of data standards (naming, quality, security, metadata) and procedures (how to request data, how to report quality issues, etc.).
2.14 Develop a Business Glossary Create and maintain repository of agreed-upon definitions for business terms, metrics, data lineage, business rules, and responsible stewards.
2.15 Coordinate with Architecture Groups Ensure DG standards align with enterprise and data architecture. Review architectural decisions for governance implications (master data, metadata, security, standards).
2.16 Sponsor Data Asset Valuation Work with finance and business to value organizational data assets using methods: replacement cost, market value, identified opportunities, selling price, risk cost.

Group 4: Embed Data Governance (Control & Operations)

Sustain and mature DG as an ongoing organizational function.

# Activity Purpose
2.17 Embed Data Governance Integrate DG into permanent organizational processes and culture. Governance becomes "how we work" rather than an overlay. Metrics tracked, stewardship roles sustained, policy compliance monitored continuously.

How to Use This Reference

  • Week 1-3: Become familiar with activities 2.1-2.4 (what needs to happen before you start DG) and 2.5-2.7 (core strategy activities).
  • Week 4-5: Deep dive into 2.9-2.11 (change management, issue management, compliance) — these are tested heavily as application scenarios.
  • Week 6: Understand how activities 2.12-2.15 connect to architecture, quality, and metadata (related KAs).
  • Week 7-8: Practice questions often ask "which activity best describes this scenario?" Know the purpose of each activity cold.

Exam Tip: Questions rarely ask "list all 17 activities" but frequently ask "which activity applies to this scenario?" Master the PURPOSE of each activity, not just the name.

Data Governance Business Drivers & Entry Points

Why do organizations invest in Data Governance? Understanding DG drivers is critical because they shape program scope, budget, stakeholder prioritization, and success metrics. Organizations don't pursue DG in a vacuum — they pursue DG when a business problem triggers the investment.

The 4 Categories of DG Business Drivers

Organizations typically initiate DG for one of four reasons:

Driver Category Why It Triggers DG Business Impact Example
Regulatory Compliance Laws/regulations require governance; audit findings; risk of penalties High financial/legal risk; potential revenue loss GDPR violation = €20M fine; BCBS 239 breach = regulatory action
Risk Reduction Data quality failures causing decisions, losses, or security incidents Business disruption; financial loss; customer trust loss Customer data breach → $50M settlement + brand damage; bad data → wrong pricing → lost revenue
Operational Efficiency Duplicate efforts, rework, integration delays due to unmanaged data Wasted time/money; slower innovation; project delays Data scientists spend 80% time cleaning data instead of analyzing; integration projects over budget due to data issues
Strategic Opportunity Data as competitive advantage; new data products; analytics initiatives Revenue opportunity; market differentiation Launch AI/ML product → needs clean master data; data monetization → needs governance

Most common initial driver: Regulatory compliance (audit findings, compliance risk).

DG Entry Points (How Programs Start)

Organizations don't launch "DG programs" in isolation. DG typically enters through one of these initiatives:

Entry Point Trigger Event DG Scope Starts Small Expands To
Data Quality Crisis Major data quality issue disrupts business (wrong prices, duplicate customers, late data) Fix the quality problem for that domain Enterprise quality governance for all domains
MDM Initiative Organization realizes customer/product duplicates are problem; needs golden record Govern master data stewardship Expand to other critical master entities
Regulatory Audit Finding Auditor finds data compliance gap (undocumented controls, unclear ownership) Remediate the specific finding Broader compliance governance across all regulated data
Data Integration Project Business wants data warehouse or data lake; realizes no standards exist Define data standards for the project Enterprise data standards and architecture governance
Cloud Migration Organization moves to cloud; realizes no data governance for cloud Govern cloud data security, compliance, ownership Data governance for all platforms (on-prem + cloud)
Privacy Regulation GDPR/CCPA hits; organization needs PII governance Implement privacy data governance Broader DG program including data quality, stewardship
Analytics/BI Initiative Business leaders want advanced analytics but trust data quality; need data governance Govern data for analytics Enterprise governance supporting all analytics use cases
Merger/Acquisition Two organizations merge; duplicate systems, conflicting data definitions Integrate master data and definitions Full DG program for combined entity

Key insight: DG programs rarely start as "comprehensive governance." They start narrow (fix one problem) then expand (embed governance more broadly).

Business Driver → DG Scope & Focus Mapping

Different drivers produce different DG programs:

Business Driver DG Program Focus Metrics That Matter Budget Allocation
Regulatory Compliance Compliance policies, audit trails, controls, evidence of governance Audit finding remediation; policy compliance %; audit readiness ~40% compliance; ~30% stewardship; ~30% tools
Risk Reduction (Security/Privacy) Security policies, access controls, encryption standards, incident response Security incidents prevented; data breach incidents; privacy violations ~50% security/access controls; ~30% stewardship; ~20% tools
Risk Reduction (Quality) Quality standards, stewardship, quality rules, metrics Data quality scores; quality issue resolution time; customer impact from quality issues ~40% stewardship; ~35% quality rules; ~25% tools
Operational Efficiency Integration standards, metadata management, process improvement Time spent on rework; project delivery speed; data integration success rate ~35% stewardship; ~35% metadata tools; ~30% standards
Strategic Opportunity Master data governance, analytics enablement, data product stewardship Data product quality; analytics model accuracy; time to insight; data product revenue ~50% stewardship; ~30% master data quality; ~20% analytics governance

How to Position DG to Different Stakeholders

Each stakeholder cares about different drivers. Smart DG leaders position DG using the driver that resonates with each stakeholder:

Stakeholder Primary Driver How to Position DG Success Metrics They Care About
CEO / Board Strategic opportunity + Risk reduction "DG enables digital transformation and new data products; mitigates regulatory/security risk" ROI; competitive advantage; risk mitigation; compliance
CFO Cost efficiency + ROI "DG prevents rework and integration costs; ROI in Year 2; data quality improves faster decision-making" Cost savings; ROI; avoidance of audit failures (regulatory fines)
Chief Risk Officer / Compliance Officer Regulatory compliance + Risk reduction "DG demonstrates compliance; audit findings remediated; risk governance embedded" Audit findings remediated; compliance demonstrated; risk metrics improving
Chief Information Security Officer Risk reduction (security/privacy) "DG governs data security and privacy; enables incident investigation; reduces breach risk" Security incidents reduced; privacy breach risk mitigated; audit readiness
CIO Operational efficiency + Risk reduction "DG standards reduce integration complexity; faster project delivery; better system design" Project delivery speed; integration complexity; technical debt reduction
Chief Data Officer All drivers "DG enables data as asset; supports all business priorities" Overall DG maturity; stewardship effectiveness; business adoption
Business Unit Leaders Operational efficiency + Strategic opportunity "DG reduces rework in your area; enables better analytics for your team; speeds up data projects" Project speed; data availability; quality for their domain

Common DG Entry Point Scenarios (Exam-Relevant)

The exam may ask: "What should DG do FIRST?" — The answer depends on the business driver:

Scenario Identified Driver DG Priority Actions
"Audit found 50 data compliance violations" Regulatory compliance Immediate: remediate findings; document controls; implement audit trails. Then: broader compliance policy.
"Customer master has 15% duplicates; causing billing errors" Risk reduction (quality) + operational efficiency Immediate: launch MDM deduplication project; appoint Master Data Steward. Then: expand to other master entities.
"GDPR took effect; we need privacy data governance" Regulatory compliance (privacy) Immediate: implement privacy data governance; map GDPR requirements to policies. Then: broader DG program.
"Data warehouse project is 6 months late due to data quality issues" Operational efficiency + risk reduction Immediate: define data quality standards for warehouse; implement quality checks. Then: enterprise quality governance.
"Organization wants to launch AI/ML product but data isn't trustworthy" Strategic opportunity Immediate: assess data quality for AI; govern master data; ensure data lineage. Then: analytics governance.
"Cloud migration happening; no governance for cloud data" Risk reduction (security/compliance) + operational efficiency Immediate: define cloud data governance standards. Then: integrated governance (on-prem + cloud).

DG Program Scope: Starts Narrow, Expands Broad

DG programs typically evolve in phases:

Phase 1: Reactive DG (Narrow Scope)
  └─ Response to specific business driver (audit finding, quality crisis, etc.)
  └─ DG focused on that domain only
  └─ Examples: "Fix customer data quality" or "Remediate compliance gap"

        ↓ (After 6-12 months of success)

Phase 2: Proactive DG (Expanding Scope)
  └─ Initial success builds credibility
  └─ DG expands to related domains
  └─ Organizational appetite grows
  └─ Examples: "Expand quality governance to all master data" or "Embed DG in SDLC company-wide"

        ↓ (After 18-24 months of maturity)

Phase 3: Strategic DG (Full Enterprise Scope)
  └─ DG embedded as permanent function
  └─ Data strategy aligns with business strategy
  └─ DG supports all 11 DMBOK KAs
  └─ Examples: "Data governance is how we work" or "DG enables digital transformation"

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "An organization has regulatory audit findings on data security. What should the DG program focus on FIRST?" (Answer: Security policies, access controls, audit trails; then expand to broader governance)
  • "A business unit wants better data for analytics but doesn't prioritize DG investment. How should CDO position DG?" (Answer: "Better analytics requires clean, trustworthy data; DG provides quality standards and stewardship to enable analytics")
  • "Two organizations merged. Customer definitions conflict; both systems have customer master. How should DG start the integration?" (Answer: Reconcile customer definitions (glossary); decide which system is authoritative; appoint Master Data Steward; dedup customers; then expand to other master entities)
  • Scenario: "Organization had a data breach. How should DG help?" (Answer: Review breach root cause (access controls, encryption gaps); define DG policies to prevent recurrence; implement governance controls; demonstrate compliance to regulators)
  • "DG program started 2 years ago fixing quality in one domain. How should it evolve?" (Answer: Expand governance to other domains; embed in SDLC; connect to business strategy; mature toward enterprise governance)

Study tip: DG programs are business-driven. The exam tests whether you understand that DG strategy varies based on business drivers, not one-size-fits-all. Be ready for scenarios where you identify the business driver and recommend the right DG entry point and focus.

DG Maturity Models — Assessment & Evolution Framework

A DG Maturity Model measures how well-developed and embedded an organization's governance practices are. Unlike a one-time readiness assessment (Activity 2.2), maturity models are used continuously to track progress and guide capability-building.

Key Distinction: Readiness vs. Maturity

Aspect Readiness Assessment Maturity Model
When Before DG program starts (one-time) Ongoing, periodic assessments (annual or quarterly)
Purpose Identify gaps before designing DG strategy Track DG program progress and capability evolution over time
Output Gap analysis + recommendations for program scope Maturity level (1–5) + roadmap to next level
Users Program sponsors deciding whether to invest in DG DG leadership measuring program effectiveness and ROI

The 5 Maturity Levels (Common Framework)

Most DG maturity models use a 5-level scale reflecting the evolution from ad-hoc to optimized:

Level Name Characteristics Governance State
1 Ad-hoc / Chaotic No formal DG; decisions made reactively; inconsistent data practices; high risk of data misuse. "We handle data problems as they come up."
2 Repeatable / Managed Basic DG policies exist; some stewards identified; DG awareness beginning; processes documented but not fully enforced. "We have some DG rules and stewards, but compliance is spotty."
3 Defined / Consistent DG policies formalized and communicated; Business Glossary in place; stewardship roles clearly assigned; DG embedded in SDLC; compliance monitored. "We have consistent DG practices across most business units."
4 Measured / Quantified DG metrics tracked and reported; DG scorecard published regularly; issues escalated formally; maturity regularly assessed. "We measure DG effectiveness and adjust based on metrics."
5 Optimized / Continuous Improvement DG embedded in culture; continuous improvement mindset; governance proactively adapts to regulatory/business changes; DG ROI demonstrated consistently. "DG is 'how we work'—constantly evolving."

Maturity Dimensions (Multi-Faceted Assessment)

Maturity is not one-dimensional. Organizations may be at different levels across different dimensions:

Dimension Level 1 Level 3 Level 5
Organizational No DG structure DGC, DGO, stewardship teams defined DG embedded in org chart; roles rotated; governance spans all BUs
Process Ad-hoc responses Policies and procedures documented Processes embedded in SDLC, hiring, budgeting
Technology No DG tools Business glossary + basic workflow tools Automated DG scorecard, integrated with data platform
People No stewards; low awareness Stewards identified; some training Stewards trained; DG literacy across all staff
Compliance Unknown regulatory gaps Regulations identified; policies drafted Full audit trails; demonstrable compliance; privacy built-in

How to Assess Maturity

A typical DG Maturity Assessment gathers data on:

  1. Governance Structure — Is there a DGC? Steering Committee? Are roles clear?
  2. Policies & Standards — Are they documented? Communicated? Enforced?
  3. Data Stewardship — Are stewards trained and active? Do they resolve issues?
  4. Business Glossary — Does it exist? Is it used? Is it current?
  5. Metrics & Monitoring — Are DG KPIs tracked? Is compliance monitored?
  6. Tool Support — Are workflow, glossary, and scorecard tools in place?
  7. Stakeholder Engagement — Do business units see DG as enabling, not blocking?
  8. Regulatory/Risk Management — Are compliance obligations met? Is risk quantified?

Results are scored (e.g., on a scale of 1–5 for each dimension), then plotted as a radar chart or heat map to visualize strengths and gaps.

Maturity Models in DMBOK2 Context

DMBOK2 doesn't name a specific proprietary maturity model but establishes the concept that DG programs mature through phases:

  • Planning phase (Readiness, Strategy) → Readiness assessment
  • Implementation phase (Policies, Stewardship, Glossary) → Early maturity
  • Embedding phase → Mature DG culture

The 3 Program Requirements (Sustainable, Embedded, Measured) map roughly to maturity:

  • Measurable programs generate metrics that enable ongoing maturity assessment.
  • Embedded programs reach Level 3-4 maturity.
  • Sustainable programs aim for Level 4-5.

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "Your DG program has defined policies and stewardship teams, but compliance is inconsistent across business units. What maturity level are you at?" (Answer: Level 2–3)
  • "Which dimension of DG maturity is least developed if stewards exist but no Business Glossary?" (Answer: Process/Technology)
  • "What is the primary difference between a readiness assessment and a maturity assessment?" (Answer: Timing and purpose — readiness is pre-launch; maturity is ongoing)
  • Scenario: "After 2 years of DG, your DG scorecard shows 75% policy compliance and DG metrics are tracked quarterly. What maturity level describes this state?" (Answer: Level 4)

Study tip: Master the distinction between "readiness" (one-time before DG) and "maturity" (ongoing after DG launch). Understand the 5 levels well enough to place an organization in a scenario.

Data Governance Business Case & ROI Justification Framework

A DG Business Case answers the fundamental question: "Why should the organization invest in DG?" It quantifies costs, benefits, and ROI in business language that executives understand — not just technical advantages, but financial impact.

Why Business Case Matters for DG

Unlike some IT projects where benefits are obvious (e.g., "faster reporting"), DG benefits are often indirect and long-term:

  • Preventing regulatory fines (not losing money vs. gaining money)
  • Reducing risk (avoiding a data breach, not preventing a feature)
  • Enabling better decisions (through trusted data)
  • Improving operational efficiency (fewer duplicate efforts, less rework)

A strong business case justifies the upfront investment and aligns DG with enterprise financial priorities.

Components of a DG Business Case

A complete business case includes:

Component Description Example
Executive Summary 1-page overview of investment, payback period, and strategic fit "3-year DG investment of $2M prevents $5M+ in regulatory risk"
Strategic Alignment How DG supports enterprise strategy and goals "Enables digital transformation by ensuring data trustworthiness"
Problem Statement Current state pain points (data quality, compliance, silos, risk) "Currently 15% of customer records have duplicates; audit found 3 policy violations"
Proposed Solution DG program scope, structure, timeline "12-month program: DGC, stewardship teams, glossary, policies, metrics"
Cost Analysis One-time and ongoing costs See Cost Elements table below
Benefit Analysis Quantified benefits across risk, efficiency, and value See Benefit Elements table below
ROI Calculation (Total Benefits — Total Costs) / Total Costs × 100% Example: ($3.5M — $2M) / $2M = 75% ROI in Year 1
Risk Mitigation Risks of not doing DG (regulatory penalty, data breaches, bad decisions) "Without DG, data breach risk increases; estimated loss: $10M+"
Timeline & Milestones Phased implementation with benefit realization schedule "Month 1-3: DG office setup; Month 4-6: policies; Month 7-12: stewardship rollout"

Cost Elements (Investment)

One-Time Costs (Year 1)

Cost Category Examples Typical Range
Personnel CDO/DG Director, DG office staff, project manager $500K–$1.5M
Technology Business glossary tool, workflow automation, DG scorecard $200K–$800K
Consulting External DG strategy/implementation support $100K–$500K
Training & Communication Steward training, stakeholder workshops, awareness campaigns $50K–$200K
Process Design Policy development, governance model design, operating framework $50K–$150K
TOTAL Year 1 $900K–$3.2M

Ongoing Costs (Year 2+, Annual)

Cost Category Examples Typical Range
Personnel DGO staff, steward time allocation (20-30% FTE), training maintainers $400K–$1M
Technology Tool licenses, maintenance, hosting, updates $100K–$300K
Operations Glossary maintenance, policy updates, issue management, metrics reporting $50K–$150K
TOTAL Year 2+ (Annual) $550K–$1.45M

Benefit Elements (Value Creation)

Risk Reduction (Quantifiable)

Benefit How Quantified Example
Regulatory Compliance Costs Avoided (Probability of fine × Fine amount) — (Post-DG risk reduction %) "40% reduction in audit findings = $2M in avoided fines over 3 years"
Data Breach Prevention (Industry avg. breach cost) × (Reduced breach probability) "DG security policies reduce breach risk by 30% = $3M savings (if breach costs $10M)"
Duplicate Data/MDM Costs Avoided Current cost of duplicate records × % solved by DG "Eliminate 15% duplicate records = $500K savings in redundant storage, effort"
Metadata/Lineage Clarity Time saved finding/trusting data vs. rebuilding it "Reduce data discovery time from 2 weeks to 2 days = $100K/year"

Efficiency Gains (Quantifiable)

Benefit How Quantified Example
Reduced Rework & Rework Hours saved per project not waiting for data clarity "30 projects/year × 40 hours saved per project × $150/hr = $180K/year"
Faster Data Project Delivery Development cycle reduction from clear standards "SDLC velocity increases 15% = $250K in faster time-to-value"
Steward Efficiency Reduction in duplicate stewardship work via glossary "One glossary vs. 5 departmental glossaries = $100K consolidation savings"
Policy/Standards Automation Automated compliance checks vs. manual review "Auto-policy enforcement reduces QA effort 20% = $75K/year"

Value Creation (Harder to Quantify, but Communicate)

Benefit How Quantified Example
Better Decision-Making Improved BI insight confidence; faster insights "Executives spend 30% less time validating data before decisions"
Competitive Advantage Speed to market for data products; data monetization "Launch new data-driven products 2 quarters earlier"
Employee Retention Reduced frustration with data quality/silos "Reduce data analyst attrition by 10% = $200K retention savings"
Strategic Alignment Data strategy aligned with business; enables digital transformation "Enables cloud migration, AI/ML initiatives by ensuring data quality"

Typical ROI Calculation Example

Scenario: Mid-size financial services company, $200M revenue, 500 employees

Investment:

  • Year 1 (one-time + staff): $1.8M
  • Year 2+ (annual): $700K

Benefits (Year 1):

  • Regulatory fine avoidance: $1.5M (estimated)
  • Data project efficiency gains: $300K
  • Reduced duplicate data costs: $200K
  • Total Year 1 Benefits: $2M

ROI Calculation:

  • Year 1 ROI = ($2M — $1.8M) / $1.8M = 11% in Year 1
  • Year 2 ROI = ($2M — $700K) / $700K = 186% in Year 2 (no one-time costs)
  • 3-Year Cumulative: ($2M + $2M + $2M) — ($1.8M + $700K + $700K) = $2.8M net benefit

Payback Period: ~10 months

How to Communicate Business Case to Different Audiences

Audience Focus Language
CFO / Finance ROI, payback period, cost avoidance, budget ownership "3-year ROI of 140%; payback in 10 months; reduces audit risk by $5M"
CEO / Board Strategic alignment, competitive advantage, risk mitigation "Enables digital transformation; prevents regulatory penalties; improves decision speed"
Business Unit Heads Efficiency gains, faster project delivery, better data for decisions "30% faster data projects; clearer responsibility for data quality; single source of truth"
Compliance / Legal Risk reduction, regulatory alignment, audit preparedness "Demonstrates compliance framework; reduces regulatory findings by 40%"
Data Teams (IT) Tool support, career growth, clearer processes "Better tools, clearer standards reduce rework; DG steward roles enable career paths"

Measuring & Tracking ROI Over Time

After DG launches, continuously track ROI using DG metrics:

Quarter 1-2 Metrics (Quick Wins)

  • # of policies approved and communicated
  • # of glossary terms defined and adopted
  • % steward training completion
  • # of issue escalations resolved (speed)

Quarter 3+ Metrics (Business Impact)

  • Regulatory audit findings (trend down)
  • Data quality scores (trend up)
  • Project delivery time (trend down)
  • Cost avoidance from prevented incidents
  • Steward satisfaction and engagement
  • Executive perception of data trustworthiness

Annual ROI Review

  • Compare actual benefits to projected benefits
  • Adjust business case for Year 2 (often higher ROI once foundations are in place)
  • Present results to executive sponsors to justify continued investment

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "A company invests $1.2M in DG Year 1 and realizes $2M in regulatory fine avoidance + efficiency gains. What is the Year 1 ROI?" (Answer: ($2M–$1.2M)/$1.2M = 67%)
  • "Which of these is the HARDEST to quantify in a DG business case?" (Answer: Competitive advantage, better decisions, employee retention)
  • "Your DG program's chief benefit is preventing a $5M regulatory penalty. How should you frame this to the CFO?" (Answer: Risk avoidance / cost prevention, not new revenue)
  • "After Year 1 of DG, annual costs drop to $700K but benefits remain $2M. Why does Year 2 ROI increase?" (Answer: One-time costs are gone; benefits continue)
  • Scenario: "You need to justify a $1.5M DG investment to a skeptical finance team. What is your strongest argument?" (Answer: Quantified risk avoidance + efficiency gains; payback period < 12 months)

Study tip: Practice converting vague DG benefits ("better data quality," "clearer responsibility") into dollar amounts. Learn to speak CFO language: cost avoidance, risk reduction, ROI, payback period.

Privacy & Data Protection Governance — Integration with DG

Privacy governance and data governance are distinct but deeply interconnected domains. Privacy focuses on protecting personal data and ensuring compliance with privacy laws (GDPR, CCPA, PIPEDA, etc.); DG focuses on managing data as an asset and ensuring quality, security, and stewardship. A mature organization integrates these two.

Key Distinction: Privacy Governance vs. Data Governance

Aspect Privacy Governance Data Governance
Focus Protecting personal data and privacy rights Managing all data as organizational asset (personal and non-personal)
Primary Driver Regulatory compliance (GDPR, CCPA, privacy laws) Multiple drivers: compliance, quality, efficiency, strategy
Scope Personal data only (PII, sensitive attributes) All data (transactional, operational, strategic)
Key Principle Lawfulness, fairness, transparency (GDPR principles) Quality, availability, security, consistency, auditability
Lead Role Data Protection Officer (DPO) or Privacy Officer Chief Data Officer (CDO) or DG Office
Primary Activities Consent management, data subject rights, retention, breach notification Stewardship, glossary, policies, standards, metrics

However: Privacy governance is a subdomain of DG. DG policies must incorporate privacy requirements.

How DG and Privacy Governance Integrate

The Data Lifecycle Integration Model

Data Collection
    ↓
[Privacy: Lawful basis, consent, purpose]
[DG: Definition, ownership, quality baseline]
    ↓
Data Processing / Storage
    ↓
[Privacy: Minimize PII, pseudonymization, access controls]
[DG: Standards, security, stewardship, glossary]
    ↓
Data Use / Sharing
    ↓
[Privacy: Purpose limitation, legitimate interest, contracts]
[DG: Policy approval, lineage, audit trails]
    ↓
Data Retention / Deletion
    ↓
[Privacy: Retention schedules, right to erasure, GDPR compliance]
[DG: Lifecycle management, archival, disposal]

At each stage, both privacy and DG governance apply.

Integration Points: Privacy in DG Activities

DG Activity Privacy Integration
2.7 Develop Goals, Principles, and Policies Include privacy principles (privacy by design, data minimization, transparency) in DG principles; reference GDPR/privacy law compliance
2.13 Sponsor Data Standards and Procedures Standards include: data classification (mark PII), access control standards, encryption, retention schedules
2.14 Develop a Business Glossary Flag which glossary terms refer to personal data; document legal basis for processing; mark retention rules for PII
2.15 Coordinate with Architecture Ensure data architecture incorporates privacy by design (PII encryption, pseudonymization, access controls)
2.11 Assess Regulatory Compliance Conduct Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA); map GDPR/CCPA/PIPEDA requirements to DG policies

CDO / DPO Collaboration Framework

A mature organization has both a CDO and a DPO (or Privacy Officer), and they collaborate on shared responsibilities:

Responsibility CDO DPO Collaboration
Data Classification & Sensitivity Leads data classification framework Reviews for PII/sensitive data identification Joint classification policy
Data Stewardship Roles Appoints and trains data stewards Ensures stewards understand privacy obligations Steward role includes privacy accountability
Data Quality & Standards Drives data quality rules and standards Ensures privacy-safe quality rules (e.g., no exposing PII) Quality rule design reviews
Retention & Lifecycle Manages data lifecycle / archival Ensures GDPR/privacy retention rules followed Data retention policy co-owned
Access Control & Security Governs data access policies Ensures need-to-know / least privilege for PII Security governance integrated
Breach Response Provides data context (what was accessed?) Leads breach notification per privacy law Incident response team includes both
Data Subject Rights Ensures data lineage/provenance documented Handles subject access requests, erasure Glossary/lineage supports SAR fulfillment
Third-Party Data Sharing Reviews data sharing contracts for quality/definitions Reviews contracts for privacy/compliance terms Data Sharing Agreements include both

Privacy-Specific DG Concepts

1. Privacy-by-Design in Data Governance

  • Data must be designed with privacy controls built-in from inception
  • Examples: encrypt PII at rest, pseudonymize in dev environments, limit access to minimum necessary roles
  • DG governance must enforce privacy-by-design in architecture and stewardship standards

2. Personal Data Handling in the Business Glossary

  • When a glossary term refers to personal data (e.g., "Customer Email," "Biometric Record"), mark it:
    • Legal basis for processing (e.g., "Contract," "Consent," "Legal Obligation")
    • Data category (e.g., "Sensitive Personal Data," "Biometric," "Children's Data")
    • Retention period (e.g., "Until customer relationship ends + 6 years" per tax law)
    • Responsible party (Data Steward + DPO contact)
    • Privacy implications (e.g., "GDPR subject to right of erasure")

3. Data Subject Rights in Stewardship

  • Data stewards must understand and facilitate GDPR/privacy law rights:
    • Right of Access — Person can request all data held about them (SAR — Subject Access Request)
    • Right of Erasure — Person can request deletion ("right to be forgotten")
    • Right to Rectification — Person can request correction of inaccurate data
    • Right to Restrict Processing — Person can limit how their data is used
    • Right to Data Portability — Person can request their data in machine-readable format
  • DG and DQ teams must be able to fulfill these requests quickly (with data lineage, glossary, metadata)

4. Consent Management & Purpose Limitation

  • Many privacy laws (GDPR, CCPA) require lawful basis for processing personal data
  • Most common lawful basis for marketing: explicit consent (person opt-in)
  • DG must track:
    • What data is collected under what consent (e.g., "Email collected for marketing consent")
    • What purposes the data can be used for (e.g., "Marketing only")
    • When consent expires or is withdrawn
  • Stewardship must prevent misuse (e.g., using marketing-only data for credit decisions)

5. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)

  • Before launching a new data initiative that processes personal data at scale, conduct a DPIA
  • DPIA evaluates:
    • Type and volume of personal data collected
    • Risk of privacy violation or data breach
    • Safeguards in place (encryption, access control, anonymization)
    • Necessity and proportionality (is the data collection necessary?)
  • DG and Privacy teams jointly conduct DPIA
  • High-risk initiatives require DPO approval before launch

Expect questions like:

  • Scenario: "An HR data steward is asked to provide a list of employees' salary data to Finance for analytics. What privacy/DG concern should DG governance flag?" (Answer: Purpose limitation — salary data collected for payroll, not analytics; lawful basis may not exist for analytics use)

Data Ethics in Governance (Focused Reference)

Data Handling Ethics is a DMBOK2 foundational topic (Chapter 2) that intersects directly with Data Governance. While the specialist exam is predominantly Data Governance (Ch 3), ethics connects to several DG concepts already in your plan: GAIP (Liability, Accountability), privacy governance, and DG principles. This focused reference covers what you need — not an exhaustive ethics treatment.

Why Ethics Matters to Data Governance

Data can be used legally but unethically. Compliance (following laws) and ethics (doing what's right) are different:

Concept Question Asked Example
Legal/Compliant "Are we allowed to do this?" "GDPR permits processing with consent"
Ethical "Should we do this, even if allowed?" "We have consent, but is using customer data to predict pregnancy and target ads appropriate?"

DG's role: Govern not just legal data use, but ethical data use. DG embeds ethical principles into policies, ensuring data is used responsibly.

DMBOK2 Core Ethical Principles for Data

DMBOK2 grounds data ethics in established principles (drawn from bioethics and the Belmont Report):

Principle Meaning DG Application
Impact on People Data ultimately represents people; mishandling harms real individuals DG policies must consider human impact of data use, not just business value
Potential for Misuse Data can be misused to harm individuals or groups DG must anticipate and prevent misuse (e.g., discriminatory profiling)
Economic Value of Ethics Ethical data handling builds trust; unethical handling destroys reputation and value DG demonstrates that ethics protects organizational value (trust = asset)

Key DMBOK ethical concepts:

  • Responsible data handling is a component of organizational social responsibility
  • Ethics must be embedded in DG culture, not treated as an afterthought
  • Organizations need an ethical data handling statement / framework (governed by DG)

How Ethics Connects to Existing DG Concepts

Existing DG Concept Ethical Connection
GAIP — Accountability Someone must be ethically accountable for data, not just legally responsible
GAIP — Liability Liability includes ethical misuse/mismanagement, not just regulatory violations (per Ch 3 summary)
Privacy Governance Privacy is partly an ethical obligation (respecting individuals) beyond legal compliance
DG Principles Ethical data handling can be embedded as a guiding DG principle
Data Policies Policies codify ethical intent (e.g., "We will not use customer data to discriminate")
Stewardship Stewards have an ethical duty to protect the data subjects represented in their data

Ethics in Modern Data Use (AI/ML, Analytics)

Modern DG increasingly governs the ethical use of data in AI/ML and analytics:

Ethical Risk Description DG Governance Response
Algorithmic Bias Models trained on biased data produce discriminatory outcomes (e.g., biased lending, hiring) DG governs data quality and representativeness; reviews data for bias before model training
Automated Decisions Decisions made by algorithms without human oversight can harm individuals DG policy: high-impact automated decisions require human review (echoes GDPR Article 22)
Profiling & Surveillance Combining data to profile individuals can be invasive even if legal DG sets boundaries on data combination; purpose limitation enforced
Re-identification "Anonymized" data can be re-identified when combined with other datasets DG governs de-identification standards; monitors re-identification risk
Consent vs. Reality People consent without understanding how data will be used DG ensures transparent, meaningful consent; ethical use beyond minimum legal consent
Data Provenance Using data of unknown or questionable origin (scraped, purchased) DG governs acceptable data sources; ethical sourcing standards

Embedding Ethics in DG: Practical Steps

A mature DG program embeds ethics through:

  1. Ethical Data Handling Statement — A governing document (like a policy) declaring the organization's ethical commitments for data use
  2. Ethics in DG Principles — Ethical considerations built into foundational DG principles
  3. Ethics Review for High-Risk Initiatives — DG reviews AI/ML, profiling, and new data uses for ethical concerns (parallel to DPIA for privacy)
  4. Steward Ethics Training — Stewards trained to recognize ethical issues, not just compliance issues
  5. Ethics Escalation Path — Ethical concerns can be raised and escalated through DG bodies (a type of issue in issue management)
  6. Culture of Ethical Data Use — DG fosters a culture where employees feel responsible for ethical data handling

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "An organization has legal consent to use customer data but the use feels invasive. What governance concern is this?" (Answer: Ethics — data can be used legally but unethically; DG must govern ethical use, not just legal compliance)
  • "GAIP 'Liability' connects to ethics how?" (Answer: Liability includes financial consequences of ethical misuse/mismanagement, not only regulatory violations)
  • "An AI model produces biased hiring recommendations. What DG governance gap allowed this?" (Answer: DG should govern data quality/representativeness and review models for bias before deployment)
  • Scenario: "Your organization wants to combine purchase data with social media data to profile customers. What should DG consider beyond legality?" (Answer: Ethical implications — is profiling invasive? Does it respect individuals? Purpose limitation; potential for misuse)
  • "What document declares an organization's ethical commitments for data handling?" (Answer: Ethical data handling statement/framework, governed by DG)

Study tip: The key exam insight is the distinction between legal compliance and ethical use — DG governs both. Ethics is "should we?" not just "can we?" Connect ethics back to GAIP (Accountability, Liability) and privacy. You don't need exhaustive ethics theory — just understand DG's role in governing ethical data use.

Chief Data Officer (CDO) Role, Accountability & Leadership Model

The Chief Data Officer (CDO) is the executive leader responsible for the entire Data Governance program — from strategy through embedding. Understanding the CDO's role, authority, accountability, and how CDO leads without direct control over all data assets is critical for the specialist exam.

Important distinction (often tested):

Authority Authority by position; governs through policy and decision rights; can escalate to CEO/Board Authority by expertise and business acumen; executes DG activities; no organizational authority line
Reporting Line Reports to CEO, CIO, or Chief Risk Officer (depends on organizational model) Reports to business (VP level) or to CDO
Tenure Permanent C-suite role (not a project manager) May be full-time DG role or part-time business responsibility

CDO Authority Model: Leading Without Direct Control

Critical concept: CDO doesn't directly manage all data assets or data teams. Instead, CDO leads through:

Authority Levers for CDO Success:

1. POLICY / STANDARDS
   └─ CDO sets data governance rules
   └─ Business units and IT must comply
   └─ Enforcement via stewardship, audit, escalation

2. EXECUTIVE SPONSORSHIP
   └─ CEO/Board support gives CDO authority to require DG participation
   └─ Budget control: CFO allocates based on CDO priorities
   └─ Strategic alignment: CEO ensures DG embedded in business strategy

3. ORGANIZATIONAL POSITION
   └─ CDO participates in executive decisions (data architecture, M&A, cloud migration)
   └─ CDO approval required for major data initiatives
   └─ CDO decision-making on data conflicts escalated to them

4. STEWARDSHIP STRUCTURE
   └─ Data stewards report to CDO (or DGC) on DG matters
   └─ Stewards have business authority; CDO has governance authority
   └─ Combined steward + CDO authority enforces DG

5. ISSUE ESCALATION
   └─ DG issues escalate to CDO's DGC for resolution
   └─ Unresolved issues escalate to CEO/Steering Committee
   └─ Escalation authority gives CDO power without direct control

Exam question type: "A data steward and a project manager disagree on data quality standards for a project. The data steward wants strict quality rules; the project manager says it will delay launch. Who has final authority?" (Answer: CDO through the DGC escalation path — not the project manager. DG policy takes precedence.)

  • Established CDO (Year 3-5) — DG embedded; business units aligned; metrics showing value; strategic influence growing
  • Strategic CDO (Year 5+) — Data strategy drives business decisions; DG culture embedded; considered trusted advisor to CEO; may move to larger org or industry role

Touchpoint How CDO Engages DG Governance Lever

Data Stewardship Program Development, Training & Maturity

"The best Data Stewards are often found, not made." However, organizations don't just find stewards lying around — they must systematically identify, recruit, train, and develop them. A mature stewardship program is the backbone of DG execution.

Steward Identification & Recruitment

How to Identify Steward Candidates

Organizations should look for stewards who have:

Characteristic Why It Matters Where to Find Them
Deep Business Knowledge Understands what data means in business context; can define business rules and reconcile conflicts Business analysts, business process owners, SMEs in each business unit
Credibility with Peers Other business users trust and listen to them; can influence without authority Often identified through peer nominations; natural leaders
Problem-Solving Mindset Sees data issues as solvable; doesn't blame IT; proactive about improvement Previous project leads; people with history of improving processes
Communication Skills Can explain data concepts to both technical and non-technical audiences People who lead meetings well; natural mentors; subject matter experts
Willingness to Learn Open to governance framework; excited about data quality; wants to improve Candidates should express interest in DG role; intrinsic motivation
Time Availability Can dedicate 10–30% of time to stewardship without overwhelming day job Typically business analysts, data analysts, not operations people 100% on urgent issues
Cross-Functional Perspective Understands how their data affects other business units; thinks enterprise-wide People with prior experience across departments

Common mistake: Assigning stewardship to someone who is an expert in the data but unpopular with peers — stewardship requires influence, not just technical knowledge.

Recruitment approach:

  1. Bottom-up nominations — Ask business units: "Who would be a good data steward for your subject area?" (often more successful than top-down assignment)
  2. Top-down appointment — For critical data domains, executives appoint Executive or Enterprise Data Stewards
  3. Hybrid model — Mix executive appointment (senior stewards) with peer nomination (subject matter stewards)

Stewardship Onboarding & Training Curriculum

The stewardship learning journey:

Phase Duration Content Outcomes
Phase 1: Orientation 1-2 weeks DG program overview; governance structure; steward roles and responsibilities; your specific domain scope Steward understands where they fit in DG organization; knows their data domain scope
Phase 2: Foundation Training 2-4 weeks DMBOK fundamentals; 7 steward types; DG principles; policies and standards; Business Glossary concepts Steward can explain DG to peers; understands compliance obligations
Phase 3: Domain Deep Dive 2-6 weeks Data lineage for their domain; data quality rules specific to their domain; related systems and dependencies; metadata standards Steward can map their data landscape; identify quality issues
Phase 4: Operational Practice Ongoing Issue escalation process; glossary entry creation; policy enforcement; conflict resolution; steward meetings Steward actively executes DG activities; resolves issues; contributes to glossary
Phase 5: Advanced Topics Months 3+ Change management for data initiatives; stakeholder influence; metrics interpretation; strategic data planning Steward becomes strategic advisor; mentors new stewards; drives proactive improvements

Training delivery methods:

  • Live workshops (interactive; builds community among stewards)
  • Recorded modules (self-paced; flexible)
  • On-the-job coaching (mentorship from Chief/Coordinating Steward)
  • Peer learning groups (stewards across domains share experiences)
  • Annual refresher training (keep stewards updated on policy changes)

Stewardship Performance Metrics & Accountability

How to evaluate if stewardship is working:

Metric How Measured Target / Expectation
Glossary Completeness % of business terms in steward's domain that have glossary entries >80% of critical business terms documented in Year 1; >95% by Year 2
Glossary Quality Average rating from glossary users (clarity, accuracy, usefulness) >4.0/5.0 rating on clarity; <10 "needs update" tags per 100 entries
Data Quality Trending % of records meeting quality standards in steward's domain Baseline in Month 1; improve by 10–20% per quarter; reach 95%+ by Year 2
Issue Resolution Speed Average time from issue report to resolution <5 business days for issues resolved at stewardship level; escalations handled faster
Policy Compliance % of data assets in steward's domain meeting governance standards >80% compliant; non-compliant assets have remediation plan
Participation & Engagement Attendance at DG meetings; contributions to glossary; initiative participation >80% meeting attendance; at least 1 glossary update per month
Steward Satisfaction Quarterly survey: Does steward feel supported? Is role clear? Do they have tools? >3.5/5.0 satisfaction; <3 = red flag (may need training, tool support, or role adjustment)
Business Impact Cost/time savings from resolved data quality issues in their domain Document savings (e.g., "avoided $50K rework by catching data error early")

Frequency: Measure monthly for real-time feedback; review quarterly with steward in 1:1 conversation.

Stewardship Career Path & Recognition

The problem: If stewardship is a thankless, unpaid addition to a steward's day job, stewards burn out and DG fails.

The solution: Build a career path and recognition program for stewards.

Stewardship Career Progression:

Tier 1: Subject Matter Data Steward
  └─ Responsible for 1 data domain / subject area (20–30% FTE)
  └─ Salary: Base salary (no increment) + DG recognition; some orgs add 5–10% bonus if metrics are strong
  └─ Advancement: Perform well as SME steward → move to Coordinating or Chief role

Tier 2: Coordinating Data Steward
  └─ Leads 3–5 subject matter stewards; represents team to DGC (30–40% FTE)
  └─ Salary: 10–15% increase; often moves to "Data Steward Manager" title
  └─ Advancement: High performers move to DGO director or Executive Steward roles

Tier 3: Executive Data Steward
  └─ Senior business leader (VP/Director level) with stewardship accountability (10–20% FTE)
  └─ Salary: C-suite level; stewardship is part of executive responsibilities
  └─ Advancement: May move to CDO or Chief Data Steward role

Tier 4: Chief Data Steward
  └─ Chairs DG Council in lieu of CDO; or Senior operational DG leader (50–100% FTE)
  └─ Salary: Senior leadership salary; likely director/VP level
  └─ Advancement: May become CDO in next role

Recognition & Incentives:

  • Formal title change — "Data Steward," "Senior Data Steward" on business card / organizational chart
  • Visible in DG scorecard — Public recognition of top-performing stewards in DG monthly report
  • DG steward awards — Annual "Data Steward of the Year" award with recognition event
  • Career path transparency — Clear communication that strong stewards can advance
  • Training budget — Sponsor steward training in metadata, quality, data science to grow skills
  • DG community — Stewards are part of an elite "data governance community" with status
  • Decision-making voice — Stewards sit on DGC; their opinions matter in organizational decisions
  • Bonus incentives — Tie annual bonuses to DG metrics (glossary completeness, quality improvement, compliance)

Key insight: Stewardship works best when it's a career, not a punishment detail.

Stewardship Maturity Progression

Stewardship maturity evolves over time as stewards become more effective:

Stewardship Maturity Level Steward Behavior Typical Timeline
Level 1: Reactive/Unaware "What is a data steward? Why am I responsible for this?" Firefighting mode. Month 1 (before training)
Level 2: Aware/Compliant "I understand the role. I follow DG policies and attend meetings. I answer questions when asked." Month 2–3 (after training; early execution)
Level 3: Proactive/Engaged "I take initiative to improve my data. I catch quality issues early. I mentor other stewards. I update glossary entries without being asked." Month 4–8 (mid-year)
Level 4: Strategic/Influencing "I advise the CDO on data strategy for my domain. I identify new opportunities for data value. I drive change across business units." Month 9–12+ (mature steward)
Level 5: Cultural Champion "DG is embedded in how I work. I influence peers to adopt DG practices. I'm a go-to expert for data governance." Year 2+ (very experienced)

Progression factors:

  • Training quality — Better training → faster progression
  • Tool support — Glossary and issue management tools → faster execution
  • Leadership support — Clear sponsorship from executive → faster adoption
  • Steward peer network — Strong steward community → knowledge sharing → faster growth
  • Time allocation — Stewards with >20% FTE dedicated → faster impact
  • Steward personality — Some stewards are naturally proactive; others need encouragement

Target: Organizations should aim to have >50% of stewards at Level 3 by end of Year 1; >70% by Year 2.

Common Stewardship Program Failures (What to Avoid)

Failure Mode Why It Happens How to Prevent It
Stewardship as punishment Assign unpopular person to stewardship role as a demotion Recruit stewards bottom-up; nominate credible people
Steward overload Assign stewardship to someone with 100% day job; stewardship becomes afterthought Carve out 15–30% FTE for stewardship; hire dedicated steward staff
No training Expect steward to figure out DG on their own; set them up for failure Invest in comprehensive onboarding and training curriculum
No tools Give stewards responsibility but no glossary tool, issue tracking, or metrics dashboards Allocate budget for DG tools; don't expect stewards to manage glossary in spreadsheets
No recognition Steward works hard, sees no reward, no career path; burns out Create career path; tie bonuses to DG metrics; publicly recognize high performers
Unclear accountability Steward doesn't know what they're accountable for; no performance evaluation Define steward responsibilities in writing; measure monthly; give feedback quarterly
Poor communication Stewards don't know DG changes, new policies, or why glossary matters Monthly steward newsletter; town halls; clear communication from CDO/DGO
Isolated stewards Subject matter stewards work in silos; no cross-domain collaboration Create steward communities of practice; monthly meetings; peer mentoring
Executive stewards missing No executives are stewards; stewardship seen as IT/admin work Appoint Executive Data Stewards from VP+ level; make stewardship part of their job description

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "You're launching a DG program. Where should you start with steward recruitment?" (Answer: Bottom-up nomination from business units; look for credible, knowledgeable people, not just experts)
  • "A newly appointed data steward says, 'I have no idea what to do.' What is the first step?" (Answer: Comprehensive onboarding and training curriculum; don't expect them to figure it out alone)
  • "A stewardship program failed because stewards quit. What was the most likely root cause?" (Answer: No recognition/career path; stewardship was seen as unpaid extra work with no benefit)
  • Scenario: "Your organization has excellent stewards at Level 3 maturity, but they are stuck there. They don't advance to Level 4. What's missing?" (Answer: Strategic engagement; stewards need to be invited into CDO/DGC decisions; need to see impact of their work)
  • "How often should steward performance be measured?" (Answer: Monthly or quarterly; not annually — too long to wait for feedback)

Study tip: Stewardship is often where DG programs succeed or fail. Be ready to discuss practical stewardship challenges: identifying stewards, training them, keeping them engaged, recognizing their work, and developing their skills over time. The exam may ask "what's wrong with this stewardship program?" scenarios.

Vendor & Third-Party Data Governance

Modern organizations increasingly rely on external data sources and vendors: cloud platforms, data-as-a-service, third-party data marketplaces, outsourced analytics, and API-based data exchanges. Vendor data governance ensures that external data meets the same quality, security, and compliance standards as internal data.

Why Vendor Data Governance Matters

Key risks with vendor data:

Risk Example Governance Control
Quality Risk Vendor's data has 30% nulls; you didn't test before integrating; impacts your BI reports Vendor data quality SLAs in contract; validation before integration; steward acceptance
Security Risk Vendor is hacked; your customer data shared with competitor; you didn't know about vendor security incidents Due diligence on vendor security; contractual breach notification; insurance requirements
Compliance Risk Vendor processes EU customer data but isn't GDPR-compliant; you're liable for violation GDPR Data Processing Agreement (DPA); vendor compliance audit before contract signing
Data Ownership Risk Vendor claims ownership of data insights generated from your data; you can't use them Clear contractual terms: you own data and derivatives; vendor has limited license only
Vendor Lock-In Risk Vendor doesn't provide data export; you can't switch vendors; dependent on proprietary format DG requirement: data must be exportable in standard format; avoid proprietary lock-in
Data Lineage Risk Data flows through vendor platform; you don't know transformations applied; can't trace lineage Requirement: vendor must document all transformations; lineage visible to your stewards

Vendor Selection & Due Diligence (Pre-Contract)

Before signing a vendor contract, conduct governance-focused due diligence:

Due Diligence Area Questions to Ask Vendor Red Flags
Data Security How do you encrypt data at rest and in transit? How do you manage access? What's your patch cycle? "We don't encrypt everything" / "We patch quarterly" = high risk
Compliance Are you SOC 2 certified? GDPR compliant? Do you have DPA template ready? Who is responsible for data subject rights requests? No certifications / evasive answers / no DPA template = risk
Data Ownership Who owns the data? Can we export it? In what format? Any restrictions? "Vendor owns data" / "Export not supported" / "Only proprietary format" = lock-in risk
Data Lineage Can you document transformations? Provide data dictionary? Support metadata standards? "We don't track transformations" = lineage opacity
Quality SLAs What data quality guarantees do you provide? Uptime? Accuracy? Refresh frequency? No SLAs / vague SLAs = poor accountability
Incident Response How do you handle data breaches? How quickly do you notify? What's your incident response process? "We'll notify when we find out" = too slow
Subprocessors Do you use other vendors for processing? Who has access to the data? Undisclosed subprocessors = hidden risk
Data Deletion How do you delete data after contract ends? How long do you retain backups? "We keep backups indefinitely" = data not truly deleted
Audit Rights Can we audit your security practices? Can we request attestations? "No audits allowed" = suspicious

Outcome: If vendor fails on critical areas (security, compliance, data ownership), either negotiate improvements or use a different vendor.

Data Governance Requirements in Vendor Contracts

A DG-aware contract should include:

Contract Clause Purpose Example Language
Data Ownership Clarify who owns the data "Customer retains all ownership of data. Vendor has limited license to process data for specified services only."
Data Protection Agreement (DPA) If personal data is processed, vendor must comply with privacy laws "Vendor shall execute GDPR Data Processing Agreement and maintain GDPR compliance."
Data Security Standards Specify minimum security controls "Vendor shall encrypt data at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+); maintain SOC 2 Type II certification."
Data Quality SLAs Define quality expectations "Vendor guarantees 99.5% data availability; maximum 5% null values in key fields; data refreshed daily."
Data Lineage & Metadata Vendor must document transformations "Vendor shall provide data dictionary, ETL documentation, and lineage for all transformations."
Compliance & Regulations Vendor responsible for meeting relevant compliance "Vendor shall maintain PCI-DSS compliance for payment data; report compliance status quarterly."
Data Export & Portability Data must be exportable in standard format "Upon contract termination, vendor shall export all customer data in CSV/Parquet format within 30 days."
Breach Notification Vendor must notify quickly if data is compromised "Vendor shall notify Customer within 24 hours of discovering a data breach."
Audit Rights You can audit vendor compliance "Customer has right to audit vendor security practices and compliance; vendor shall provide SOC 2 reports annually."
Subprocessor Notification You know if vendor uses other vendors "Vendor shall notify Customer of any subprocessors; Customer may object to subprocessors."
Data Deletion Vendor must delete data after contract ends "Upon contract termination, Vendor shall securely delete all Customer data within 30 days; provide deletion certification."
Liability & Insurance Vendor liable if data is mishandled "Vendor shall maintain cyber liability insurance of $X million covering data breaches."
Term & Exit Strategy Contract terms and offboarding process "Contract is 3-year term; 60-day notice for termination; vendor provides data export and transition support."

Managing External Data Quality

When data comes from a vendor, quality governance changes:

Phase DG Activity Responsibility
Pre-Integration Request vendor data samples; run quality validation tests; confirm SLAs Your DG team + vendor
Integration Implement data quality rules specific to vendor data; monitor incoming data quality daily Your DQ stewards + vendor
Ongoing Track vendor data quality metrics; escalate issues; vendor response SLA is 48 hours Your stewards (owner is vendor data steward)
Disputes If vendor data quality misses SLA, invoke contract remedies (credit, termination) CDO / contract manager

Example vendor data quality scenario:

  • SLA: "Vendor will provide clean customer records with <1% duplicates"
  • Reality: Month 1 data has 5% duplicates
  • Action: Escalate to vendor; they investigate and promise fix in Month 2
  • Month 2: Still 4% duplicates
  • Resolution: Vendor credits you for SLA miss; you implement deduplication before using their data; or you switch vendors

Cloud Data Governance Specifics

Cloud vendors (AWS, Azure, GCP) are major data hosts. DG requirements include:

Cloud Governance Area Requirement Why It Matters
Data Residency Where is data physically stored? (EU data in EU per GDPR; healthcare data in compliant regions) Regulatory requirement; some orgs restrict data geography
Encryption Keys Who owns encryption keys? (You or cloud provider?) If provider owns keys, they could decrypt your data; DG prefers customer-owned encryption keys
Access Control How are cloud resources accessed? (IAM roles, IP restrictions, MFA?) Prevents unauthorized access; DG should define cloud access policies
Audit Logging Does cloud provider log all access to your data? Can you access audit logs? Compliance audits require proof of who accessed data and when
Data Classification Which data can go in cloud? (Sensitive data sometimes restricted to on-prem) DG policy should specify what data types are cloud-eligible
Backup & Recovery How does vendor backup your data? Can you restore quickly? RPO (Recovery Point Objective) and RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defined in contract
Multi-Tenancy Risk Could other cloud customers accidentally access your data? DG requires vendor isolation guarantees; SLA for tenant isolation
Cost Governance Cloud storage grows; how do you prevent runaway costs? DG can define data retention policies (delete old data) to control costs

Data Ownership & Liability When Using Vendors

Key question: If something goes wrong, who is liable?

Scenario Data Ownership Liability
Vendor is hacked; your data is stolen You own data; vendor has limited license Vendor is liable (breach of contract, negligence); you may pursue damages
Vendor's transformations corrupt your data You own data; vendor made the error Vendor is liable for data loss; you have right to remediation/credit
You requested vendor delete data; they didn't You own data; vendor failed to delete Vendor is liable for GDPR/compliance violations; you could face regulatory fines
Vendor goes out of business You own data; vendor must export it Your contract requires data export before shutdown; vendor should have DPA covering data deletion
You use vendor data in a way that violates privacy Vendor provided data; you used it wrong You are liable (misuse of data); vendor is not liable for how you use their data

DG strategy: Include liability clauses in vendor contracts; require vendor insurance; conduct due diligence before signing.

Preventing Vendor Lock-In Through DG Governance

Vendor lock-in occurs when you can't easily switch vendors because:

  • Data is in proprietary format; you can't export it
  • Transformations are encoded in vendor's proprietary language; you can't replicate them elsewhere
  • You have no documentation of data lineage; you don't know what vendor did to your data

DG prevention controls:

Control How It Works Benefit
Data Portability Requirement Contract requires data export in standard format (CSV, Parquet, JSON) You can switch vendors; data is portable
Documentation Requirement Vendor documents all transformations, ETL logic, business rules You understand what vendor did; you can replicate elsewhere
Open Data Standards Use standard data formats, not proprietary ones Data works across multiple vendors; not locked to one
Metadata Governance Your stewards own the glossary; vendor data mapped to your terms You own semantic understanding; not dependent on vendor's definitions
Source Code Escrow If vendor goes out of business, you get source code of their ETL You can maintain/migrate data yourself; no data loss
Regular Data Audits Periodically export data and verify you can restore it elsewhere Validates portability; catches lock-in before it's too late

  • "Your vendor is hacked and customer data is exposed. Who is liable?" (Answer: Primarily the vendor (breach of contract); however, you may have liability too if you failed to vet vendor security (due diligence failing))
  • Scenario: "You want to switch cloud vendors, but your data is in the vendor's proprietary format and they won't export it. How could you have prevented this?" (Answer: DG should require data export in standard format in the contract; maintain portable data)
  • "A vendor provides master data but doesn't document transformations. What stewardship problem does this create?" (Answer: Data lineage is unclear; stewards can't understand data quality issues; can't validate vendor work)

Data Quality Governance Integration

Data Quality (DQ) and Data Governance (DG) are complementary but distinct disciplines. DG governs quality; DQ executes quality improvements. Understanding how they integrate is critical for the specialist exam and real-world DG leadership.

DG vs. DQ: Distinction & Integration

Aspect Data Governance Data Quality
Focus Authority, policy, stewardship, oversight Measurement, remediation, improvement
Question Asked "Who is accountable for this data?" "What policies govern its use?" "How clean is this data?" "How do we fix the quality issues?"
Primary Role Data Steward (business accountability) Data Quality Analyst (technical execution)
Primary Activity Define quality standards and policies Implement DQ rules, run quality checks, report metrics
Timeframe Strategic (quality baseline set once, reviewed annually) Operational (quality checks run continuously; issues reported daily)
Authority Steward approves quality standards Analyst executes what steward approved
Escalation Quality issues that violate policy escalate to DG Council Quality metrics tracked; escalates if trend worsens

The Integration: DG sets the standard ("Customer records must have <2% nulls in key fields"); DQ measures and reports ("Current null rate is 3%; we're out of compliance"); DG escalates and resolves ("Why are we failing the standard? What actions fix it?").

The Quality Governance Framework

DG establishes the framework; DQ operates within it:

DG Level (Policy & Accountability)
  ├─ Define quality dimensions (accuracy, completeness, timeliness, consistency)
  ├─ Set quality standards for each data domain (e.g., "Customer records: 99% accuracy, <1% nulls")
  ├─ Assign data steward (accountable for quality in domain)
  ├─ Establish quality metrics and thresholds
  └─ Escalation path (quality issue → steward → DGC → Steering Committee)

        ↓ (delegates to)

DQ Level (Execution & Measurement)
  ├─ Implement quality rules (business rules, validation rules, data profiling)
  ├─ Run quality checks (daily/hourly profiling, validation against standards)
  ├─ Report quality metrics (dashboard, scorecard, alerts)
  ├─ Investigate root causes (why did quality degrade?)
  └─ Recommend remediation (data cleansing, process fixes, system changes)

        ↓ (reports back to)

DG Level (Oversight & Decision-Making)
  ├─ Steward reviews quality metrics (is trend improving?)
  ├─ Steward approves remediation plans (how do we fix the quality issues?)
  ├─ Steward resolves quality conflicts (which standard takes priority if two standards conflict?)
  └─ Steward tracks quality baseline improvement (quarter-over-quarter trends)

Quality Standards & Policy: Who Defines, Who Enforces

Critical distinction (often tested):

Artifact Defined By Enforced By Change Control
Quality Standards Business Data Steward (with input from DQ analysts) DQ analyst (implements rules, monitors) DG Council approves changes; steward reviews annually
Quality Rules Business Steward + DQ Analyst (technical translation) Automated system (DQ tool runs checks) DQ analyst implements; steward approves
Quality Metrics & Thresholds Steward (what matters to business?) + DQ analyst (what's measurable?) DQ tool (auto-calculates metrics) Steward can adjust thresholds; DQ analyst adjusts how metrics are calculated
Quality Policies DG Office (CDO/DGC approves) All stewards + DQ teams (must follow) DG governance process (quarterly review)

Example scenario:

  • Steward says: "Customer records must be accurate. I want 99% of customer names to be correct."
  • DQ analyst translates: "Let's implement fuzzy match validation. If customer name differs from source by <2 characters, flag it."
  • Rule implemented: Validation rule in data pipeline; runs on all customer records daily
  • Metric reported: 98.5% of records pass the rule; 1.5% flagged as potentially inaccurate
  • Steward action: Approves remediation plan to contact customers with potential errors; goal is to reach 99% by end of quarter

Quality issues that can't be resolved operationally escalate through DG governance:

Master Data Governance & DG Integration

Master Data Management (MDM) creates and maintains "golden records" — authoritative, high-quality versions of critical business entities (customers, products, suppliers, accounts, employees). Data Governance sets the rules for how master data is created, maintained, and used. MDM is where DG governance is most visible and most critical to business success.

MDM vs. DG: Distinction & Integration

Aspect Master Data Management Data Governance (applied to MDM)
Focus Creating and maintaining golden records; data consolidation and deduplication Authority, stewardship, quality standards, policy for master data
Question Asked "What is the authoritative customer record?" "How do we reconcile duplicates?" "Who owns the customer master data?" "What quality standards must it meet?"
Primary Role MDM architect, MDM analyst, data steward (who owns the golden record) Master Data Steward (business accountability for master data quality)
Primary Activity Data consolidation, matching/deduplication, survivorship rules, golden record creation Stewardship, policy, standards, quality governance, accountability
Scope Specific master domains (customers, products, accounts, suppliers, employees, locations) All master domains; how they integrate with DG framework

The Integration: DG defines governance standards for master data (highest priority); MDM implements those standards through deduplication, matching, survivorship rules. Master data is the highest-governance domain — it often determines business decisions and revenue.

Why Master Data Is Highest-Priority DG Governance

Master data is critical because:

Reason Business Impact
Revenue Impact Wrong customer data = wrong address = lost orders; wrong product data = wrong pricing; wrong account data = wrong billing
Regulatory Impact Customer master must comply with privacy regulations; inaccurate master data can violate compliance
Operational Impact Every business process depends on master data; poor master data cascades across entire organization
Decision Impact Executives make decisions based on customer/product data; wrong master data = wrong decisions
Integration Impact All data warehouses, BI systems, analytics depend on clean master data as foundation

Result: Master data quality issues are often more visible and more critical than other data quality issues. When customer master is dirty, business users notice immediately.

Master Data Stewardship: The Role

Master Data Stewardship is different from (and more senior than) regular data stewardship:

Characteristic Regular Data Steward Master Data Steward
Domain Scope One operational data domain (e.g., "Customer Transactions") One master entity (e.g., "Customer Master" across entire organization)
Stakeholder Breadth Primarily one business unit Cross-functional — all business units that use customer master
Authority Level Business analyst level; works with stewardship team Executive or senior level (VP or Director); often chairs cross-functional committee
Conflict Resolution Resolves issues within domain Resolves conflicts across business units on what constitutes "the customer"
Accountability Responsible for data stewardship activities in their domain Personally accountable for master data quality org-wide
Decision Making Advises on policies; implements decisions Makes strategic decisions on master data approach, investment, standards

Example conflict a Master Data Steward resolves:

  • Sales says: "Customer master should include all prospects (potential customers)"
  • Finance says: "No, master should only include paying customers"
  • Master Data Steward decides: "We'll have two customer types in master: Prospect and Active; separate processes for each; single consolidated record with type indicators"
