MDM Investment Never Justified MDM is expensive; business doesn't understand ROI; gets defunded DG must quantify master data value (revenue impact, cost of duplicates) in business case

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "In an organization with multiple business units using customer data, who should be the Master Data Steward?" (Answer: Senior executive (VP/Director) from business; must be cross-functional; not IT person)
  • "Master customer data has 5% duplicate rate. Who is accountable for improving this?" (Answer: Master Data Steward; steward approves deduplication rules and monitors trending)
  • "What quality standard should master data meet compared to operational data?" (Answer: Master data standards are STRICTER (99%+ vs. 95%); higher business impact)
  • Scenario: "Sales wants all prospects in customer master; Finance wants only paying customers. How should DG handle this conflict?" (Answer: Master Data Steward defines customer types; implements as 'Active' vs. 'Prospect' in master; documents in policy)
  • "An organization created an MDM system but master data quality is still poor. What governance is missing?" (Answer: Master Data Steward governance; policies; quality standards; steward accountability; metrics tracking)

Study tip: Master data governance is where DG is MOST visible and MOST impactful. The exam tests whether you understand that MDM implementation (matching, deduplication, survivorship) is technical work, but MDM governance (stewardship, policy, standards, conflict resolution) is where DG adds value. Be ready for real-world master data conflicts and how DG stewardship resolves them.

Data Architecture Governance & DG Integration

Data Architecture is the design and blueprint for how data flows, is stored, and is used across the organization. Data Governance sets the rules and standards that architecture must follow. Activity 2.15 (Coordinate with Architecture Groups) is where DG and architecture explicitly integrate.

Data Architecture vs. DG: Distinction & Integration

Aspect Data Architecture Data Governance (applied to Architecture)
Focus Design of data systems, models, flows, and structures Standards, policies, and accountability for architecture decisions
Question Asked "How should we structure this data?" "What's the best architecture for this need?" "Does this architecture comply with DG standards?" "Who is accountable for data in this architecture?"
Primary Role Data Architect (technical design) Data Steward (business accountability); Architecture Steward (if exists)
Primary Activity Design databases, data models, integration patterns, data flows Define architecture standards, review designs for compliance, approve architecture decisions
Scope Technical design of all data systems and flows DG governance of architecture; ensuring it supports data quality, security, stewardship

The Integration: DG sets architecture standards (e.g., "All customer data must support real-time replication"); Architecture implements those standards (e.g., "We'll use change data capture for real-time sync").

Architecture Governance Framework

DG establishes the governance framework; Architecture executes it:

DG Level (Standards & Governance)
  ├─ Define data architecture standards and principles
  ├─ Establish architecture governance policies
  ├─ Assign Architecture Steward (if large org)
  ├─ Review major architecture decisions for DG compliance
  ├─ Ensure architecture supports data quality, security, lineage requirements
  └─ Escalate architecture conflicts to DGC

        ↓ (delegates to)

Architecture Level (Design & Execution)
  ├─ Design systems that meet DG standards
  ├─ Create data models that support stewardship
  ├─ Implement data lineage and metadata capture
  ├─ Design for data quality (validation at source, data profiling)
  ├─ Design for security (encryption, access control, audit logging)
  └─ Report architecture metrics to DG

        ↓ (reports back to)

DG Level (Oversight & Decision-Making)
  ├─ Steward reviews architecture decisions
  ├─ Steward ensures architecture supports data stewardship
  ├─ Steward approves architecture changes that impact governance
  └─ Steward escalates architectural conflicts (e.g., performance vs. governance)

Key Architecture Governance Decisions

DG weighs in on critical architecture decisions:

Architecture Decision DG Governance Aspect Question DG Asks
Database Selection (SQL vs. NoSQL) Data quality, lineage, auditability "Can we track data lineage? Support audit trails? Enforce quality rules?"
Cloud vs. On-Premise Data security, compliance, residency "Where does data reside? Can we audit access? Meet compliance requirements?"
Real-Time vs. Batch Processing Data freshness, quality, timeliness "What data freshness does the business need? Can we meet SLAs?"
Data Lake vs. Data Warehouse Data governance, metadata, stewardship "How do we govern data lake data? Track lineage? Enforce quality?"
API-Based vs. ETL Integration Data lineage, security, standards compliance "Can we trace data from source? Enforce encryption? Monitor access?"
Master Data Location Stewardship, quality accountability "Where does master data live? Who's accountable? How do we update it across systems?"
Data Model Design Stewardship, metadata, quality "Does model support business glossary? Enable quality rules? Support data lineage?"

Architecture Standards Governance

DG defines architecture standards that all projects must follow:

Architecture Standard DG Purpose Example
Data Classification Standard Ensure all data is classified (public, internal, confidential, restricted) "All PII must be marked as 'Restricted'; encryption required"
Encryption Standards Security and compliance requirement "All customer data encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest (AES-256)"
Audit Logging Standard Enable compliance and investigation "All master data changes logged with user, timestamp, before/after values"
Data Quality Rules Standard Quality enforcement at system level "All customer names validated for length/format before database insert"
Metadata Capture Standard Enable lineage and stewardship "All ETL processes must capture source, transformations, target; metadata must be in glossary"
Data Lineage Standard Enable impact analysis and troubleshooting "All data transformations must be documented; lineage visible in metadata tool"
API Data Standards Ensure external data integrations meet standards "All API integrations must validate data format, completeness, timeliness before acceptance"

Architecture Stewardship Role

In large organizations, an Architecture Steward or Data Architecture Steward may exist:

Responsibility How It Executes
Define Architecture Standards Work with architects and DG to document what architecture approaches are approved
Review Architecture Designs Before major projects launch, steward reviews design for DG/standards compliance
Ensure Metadata Capture Ensure data lineage and metadata are captured in architecture (enables stewardship)
Resolve Architecture Conflicts When architect and DG steward disagree (performance vs. governance), escalate to DGC
Track Architecture Metrics Monitor: % of systems meeting DG standards; time to implement DG features; architecture governance compliance

Common Architecture Governance Failures

Failure Mode Why It Happens How to Prevent
No Architecture Governance DG doesn't review architecture; architects build what they want DG must have approval authority for major architecture decisions
Architecture Doesn't Support Lineage Architects don't think about metadata; no way to track data flow DG standard: "All systems must capture and report data lineage"
Poor Data Model Design Model doesn't match business glossary; stewards can't use it Steward reviews data model; ensures it aligns with business definitions
No Audit Logging Security/compliance requirement missed; can't investigate data issues DG policy: "All data changes must be logged"
Encryption Inconsistent Some systems encrypt, some don't; no standard DG standard: "All PII must be encrypted; document key management"
Data Quality Not Built-In Quality validation added later (expensive); poor data flows through systems DG requirement: "Quality rules must be at source; validated on insert"
Lineage Invisible After launch, no one knows where data came from; hard to troubleshoot DG standard: "All transformations documented; lineage visible in metadata tool"

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "Which architecture decision requires DG governance approval?" (Answer: Major decisions affecting data quality, lineage, security, compliance, stewardship — cloud migration, master data location, data model design)
  • "A project wants to use a NoSQL database for customer data but DG is concerned about audit trails. What's the DG concern?" (Answer: NoSQL may not support audit logging of changes; DG requirement is to track all data modifications)
  • "Data lineage is invisible in your current architecture. Why is this a governance problem?" (Answer: Stewards can't troubleshoot quality issues; compliance can't trace data for audits; can't manage data dependencies)
  • Scenario: "An architect proposes real-time streaming but DG needs batch validation. How does DG resolve this?" (Answer: DG works with architect to find hybrid approach — real-time ingest + batch validation; architecture must support governance needs)
  • "Who should review and approve architecture decisions for DG compliance?" (Answer: DG steward or architecture steward; escalates to DGC if conflict with architect)

Study tip: Architecture governance is where DG influences how systems are built. The exam tests whether you understand that DG can't dictate architecture choices, but DG can set governance requirements that architecture must meet. Be ready for scenarios about architecture decisions and their governance implications.

Metadata Governance & DG Integration

Metadata is "data about data" — information that describes what data is, where it is, how it's structured, who uses it, and how it flows. Metadata Governance is how DG manages metadata as a strategic asset. The Business Glossary is one application of metadata governance, but there's much more.

Metadata vs. Glossary: Distinction

Type Scope Owner Purpose
Business Metadata (Glossary) Business terms, definitions, business rules, metrics Business Steward Common business understanding
Technical Metadata Data structures, field names, data types, database locations Technical Data Steward / DBA System design and integration
Operational Metadata Data refresh schedules, SLAs, lineage, transformation logic Data stewards + operators Day-to-day operations
Quality Metadata Quality rules, quality metrics, data profiling results Data Quality team + steward Quality management
Security Metadata Classification, encryption, access controls, audit logs Security + steward Compliance and access control

Business Glossary is the most visible metadata, but metadata governance encompasses all of these.

Metadata Governance Framework

DG establishes standards for all metadata types:

DG Level (Metadata Governance)
  ├─ Define metadata standards (what metadata must be captured, in what format)
  ├─ Assign Metadata Steward (typically DGO director or senior steward)
  ├─ Establish metadata governance policies
  ├─ Ensure metadata is captured and maintained
  ├─ Link metadata to stewardship (who owns this data?)
  └─ Use metadata to enable all DG activities

        ↓ (delegates to)

Metadata Management Level (Execution)
  ├─ Implement metadata tool/glossary
  ├─ Capture metadata from systems (lineage, data models, transformations)
  ├─ Maintain business glossary entries
  ├─ Link technical metadata to business glossary
  ├─ Update metadata when systems/processes change
  └─ Report metadata quality metrics

        ↓ (reports back to)

DG Level (Oversight & Usage)
  ├─ Steward reviews metadata quality
  ├─ Use metadata for impact analysis (if I change this field, what else breaks?)
  ├─ Use metadata for compliance (trace data for audits)
  ├─ Use metadata to enable stewardship (glossary helps stewards do their job)
  └─ Escalate metadata gaps (missing lineage, undefined terms)

The 5 Metadata Dimensions (Complete Picture)

Complete metadata governance covers all dimensions:

Dimension What It Includes Example
Structural Metadata Schema, tables, columns, data types, relationships Customer table has: CustomerID (int), Name (varchar 100), Email (varchar 50)
Descriptive Metadata Business definitions, glossary entries, business rules "Customer = legal entity with at least one completed purchase"
Operational Metadata Lineage, data flow, refresh schedules, dependencies, SLAs Customer data refreshed daily at 2am; fed from 3 source systems; updated to 45 downstream systems
Quality Metadata Data quality rules, quality metrics, data profiling Customer Name: required, no nulls, max 100 chars; 98.5% currently passing
Governance Metadata Ownership, stewardship, access controls, sensitivity classifications, compliance mappings Owner: Sarah Chen; Classified as "Internal"; GDPR applies (customer PII); PCI-DSS applies (if payment card linked)

Key Metadata Governance Responsibilities

Responsibility Who Does It Measures Success
Define Metadata Standards DG/Metadata Steward Standards documented; all systems follow them
Capture Metadata Technical team + metadata tool >90% of systems have their metadata captured
Maintain Metadata DGO + stewards Metadata current; <5% of entries are stale
Ensure Metadata Accuracy Data stewards (validate business terms, rules) Glossary entries are accurate; users trust them
Enable Metadata Discovery Metadata tool with search/navigation Users can find data they need; >80% of searches successful
Link Metadata Across Domains Metadata team + stewards Technical schema linked to business glossary; lineage connects source to target
Use Metadata for Stewardship Data stewards Stewards use glossary for quality rules; lineage for impact analysis
Govern Metadata Access DG/Security PII in metadata (e.g., data locations) restricted to authorized users

Data Lineage Governance (Critical)

Data lineage is metadata that shows how data flows through systems. DG governance of lineage is critical:

Lineage Governance Aspect Why It Matters Example
Source Identification Stewards must know where data originates Customer data comes from: Salesforce (primary) + manual entry (secondary)
Transformation Capture Understanding what happens to data between source and use Customer name: trimmed + uppercase in ETL before loading to warehouse
Dependency Mapping Understanding what breaks if you change something If customer ID format changes, 23 downstream reports break
Compliance Tracing Demonstrating data compliance for audits PII trace: Customer PII in source → encrypted in transit → masked in dev → unencrypted in prod (gap!)
Troubleshooting Quick identification of data quality issues If customer name is wrong: trace from source → identify which ETL step introduced error
Impact Analysis Before changing a system, understand ripple effects Before replacing Salesforce: identify all processes/reports that depend on Salesforce data

Metadata Governance Challenges

Challenge Why It's Hard How DG Addresses It
Metadata Sprawl Metadata exists in many tools (databases, BI tools, data dictionaries, wikis); no central source of truth DG standard: "Single glossary tool is authoritative; all systems reference it"
Stale Metadata Systems change; metadata isn't updated; glossary entries become inaccurate DG policy: "When system changes, metadata must update within 5 days"
Lineage Invisible ETL tools don't capture lineage; custom scripts have no documentation DG standard: "All transformations must be documented; lineage visible in metadata tool"
Technical-Business Gap Technical metadata (database columns) doesn't align with business metadata (glossary terms) Metadata steward maps technical fields to glossary terms; ensures alignment
Metadata Not Used Glossary exists but stewards don't use it; low adoption DG must market metadata; integrate into daily work (e.g., stewards use lineage for troubleshooting)
Metadata Security Sensitive metadata (data locations, quality metrics) exposed to unauthorized users DG policy: "Metadata access controlled; sensitive data locations restricted"
Metadata in Silos Each business unit has own glossary; no enterprise view; conflict on definitions DG must consolidate: one enterprise glossary; business units contribute but DG governs

Metadata Governance Maturity

Maturity Level Metadata Governance State
Level 1: Ad-Hoc No centralized metadata; data descriptions scattered in emails, wikis, heads of people; lineage unknown
Level 2: Reactive Some metadata captured in tools; glossary started but incomplete; lineage partially documented
Level 3: Proactive Comprehensive metadata captured; glossary actively maintained; lineage tracked for major data flows
Level 4: Optimized All metadata integrated; technical and business metadata linked; lineage automated; metadata enables stewardship
Level 5: Strategic Metadata is strategic asset; enables AI/ML (data discovery), compliance automation (lineage for audits), data products

Exam Relevance

Expect questions like:

  • "What is the difference between a Business Glossary and Metadata Governance?" (Answer: Glossary is one type of business metadata; metadata governance is broader — includes technical, operational, quality, governance metadata)
  • "A steward can't find data lineage for a customer field. Why is this a governance problem?" (Answer: Can't troubleshoot quality issues; can't trace for compliance; can't do impact analysis if system changes)
  • "Your organization has 5 different glossaries (one per business unit) with conflicting definitions of 'Customer.' What governance is missing?" (Answer: Enterprise metadata governance; DG must enforce one glossary with business unit input)
  • Scenario: "A system is replaced but metadata isn't updated. Two weeks later, stewards are using wrong definitions. How should DG prevent this?" (Answer: DG policy: metadata updates required within 5 days of system change; steward owns verification)
  • "Metadata is captured but no one uses it. What should DG do?" (Answer: Metadata must be integrated into steward work — lineage for troubleshooting, glossary for standard definitions; low adoption indicates metadata doesn't solve real problems)

Study tip: Metadata governance is foundational to ALL stewardship work. The exam tests whether you understand that metadata enables stewardship — without accurate metadata, stewards can't do their jobs. Be ready for scenarios about metadata completeness, accuracy, and how to govern it.
